Preface
The present day Chemistry laboratory has the following 
features:
•	 lot	 of	wastage	of	chemicals	and	increased	cost	of	 	
setting up and maintaining chemistry laboratory.
•	 increased	 water	and	air	pollution	due	to	excessive	use	
of	chemicals	and	obnoxious	and	toxic	fumes,	leading	
to environmental pollution.
•	 many	accidents	due	to	fire	and	hazardous	chemicals.
•	 cook-book	 approach	to	practicals,	giving	little	time	
for	thinking,	increases	information	load	rather	than	
clarifying the concepts.
How	 to	 maintain	 a	 pollution-free	 environment,	 how	
to cut chemistry laboratory costs and to handle chemical 
wastes are the present day concerns. These concerns have 
been addressed by designing and developing an alternative 
way	of	performing	chemistry	experiments	in	the	laboratory	
known	 as	 Microscale	 Chemistry	 laboratory Techniques. 
It may be mentioned that the present Kit, based on the 
National	Curriculum	Framework	(NCF),	highlights	the	use	of	
microscale chemistry techniques in schools.
We have developed special apparatus, which limits 
the volume of liquid reagent and the quantity of the solid 
chemicals used without compromising on the observation 
skills,	chemical	principles	involved,	accuracy,	etc.	Moreover,	
doing	chemistry	experiments	this	way	saves	costly	heating	
system based on gas burners in traditional laboratories.
Volumetric	methods	have	been	simplified	and	physical	
chemistry	experiments	could	now	be	done	using	this	Kit,	
which, otherwise, are hardly done in schools. Conventional 
laboratory wares are replaced by items based on microscale 
chemistry.
We hope this Kit will be useful for students, teachers and 
schools.	Feedback	for	improving	this	Kit	is	welcome.
 R.K. Parashar
New Delhi       Professor
October 2017  Division of Educational Kits

IntroductIon to MIcroscale 
cheMIstry laboratory KIt
The crucial role of practical work and experimentation in 
science curriculum is universally accepted. This is more 
so in chemistry, which is an experimental science. Most of 
the concepts in this area are better understood by doing  
practical work.
The aims and objectives of practical work in the laboratory 
can be stated as follows:
•	 better understanding of scientific concepts and 
principles.
•	 promotion of basic skills and competencies (procedural 
and manipulative skills, observational skills, drawing 
skills, reporting and interpretation skills).
•	 awakening and maintaining curiosity in the learning 
environment.
Laboratory work is an indispensable part of chemistry 
instructions. Despite several laudable efforts in the 
past, experiments, by and large, have continued to be 
marginalised in school education and have not received 
due importance. There are several factors which contribute 
towards the neglect of laboratory work. In particular, there 
is	a	crunch	of	financial	resources	for	developing	a	separate	
conventional chemistry laboratory. The increasing cost of 
chemicals, handling a large number of students, no time to 
maintain equipment and accessories, no money to replace 
breakages, problems in the disposal of waste, handling 
toxic chemicals and working in shifts are some other major 
contributing factors.
 In order to overcome the above problems, the desired 
modifications	may	be:
•	 change in facilities.
•	 modifications	in	laboratory	programmes.	
•	 optimisation in the use of resources.

Manual of Microscale cheMistry laboratory Kit
•	 adaptation	of	cost-effective,	safe	and	efficient	techniques.	
a move towards ‘green chemistry’.
Alternative ideas to replace the conventional laboratory, while meeting the 
objectives of practical work, are being thought of. Recent developments 
include microscale chemistry experiments using small quantity of 
chemicals and simple equipment. The concept was first introduced by 
D.W. Mayo, S.S. Butcher, et al. at Bowdoin College in Brunswick about 30 
years ago. In India, this concept has been developed and introduced in the 
school system by the NCERT with some innovative laboratory apparatus 
in the form of a kit known as Microscale Chemistry Laboratory Kit.
I. What Is MIcroscale cheMIstry laboratory 
   (Mcl) KIt? 
The Microscale chemistry Laboratory Kit enables students 
to perform experiments in an environmentally safe and  
pollution-free atmosphere, using small quantities of chemicals 
without compromising with the quality and standard of 
experiments. The experiments can be performed easily and 
quickly. They are safer and less polluting. The bigger size 
reagent bottles, glassware, plasticware, etc., in a conventional 
laboratory are being replaced by their smaller size counterparts. 
In short, this method is cost-effective, student, environment, 
administrator and teacher-friendly.
II. advantages of usIng the KIt
The M cL Kit uses solid chemicals in quantities of a few 
milligrams and liquid chemicals in few drops using special 
low-cost apparatus.
1. student-frIendly 
•	 The use of chemicals in small quantities reduces fumes 
and risk of accidents, acid burns, etc.
•	 The experiments are quick to perform, thus, saving 
time for performing more experiments.
•	 It develops the habit of conservation.

•	 It reduces use of chemicals resulting in waste reduction 
at the source.
•	 It offers vastly enhanced laboratory safety by improving 
the laboratory air quality through reduction in:
 ◦ exposure to toxic chemicals.
 ◦ fire	and	explosion	hazards.
 ◦ spills and accidents.
3. adMInIstrator-frIendly
•	 It sharply reduces laboratory cost.
•	 It lowers glass breakage cost.
•	 It saves storage space.
4. teacher-frIendly
•	 It promotes better student discipline in the laboratory.
•	 It is pedagogically sound. Teachers can ask the 
students to do more experiments during the saved 
time to help in better conceptual understanding.
III. What specIal apparatus are provIded In the KIt?
Following is a list of some special apparatus provided:
 1. Small portable box for easy transportation of apparatus, 
and their storage.
 2. Polyethylene dispensing bottles (squeeze type) to dispense 
liquid chemicals dropwise avoiding the contamination  
of chemicals.
 3. Well plates for performing tests. 
 4. W-tubes for generating gases in small quantities and 
studying their properties.
 5. Barrel pipettes.
 6. Miniature glassware for the minimum consumption  
of chemicals.
	 7.	 Micro	filtration	unit.
 8. Micro spatulas.

prIMary and secondary standards
A standard solution is one whose concentration is known 
accurately. A standard solution of an acid/base is used 
to determine the unknown concentration of a solution of 
base/acid by volumetric analysis. There are various ways 
of expressing the concentration of a standard solution. The 
concentration of a standard solution is usually expressed in 
moles per litre (molarity). For example, a standard solution 
of oxalic acid can be used to determine the unknown 
concentration of an alkali solution. The formula of hydrated 
crystalline oxalic acid is:

experIMent 2.2
To determine the strength of a given solution of Sodium 
hydroxide by titrating it against a standard solution of  
oxalic acid.
theory
In the titration of o xalic acid (weak acid) against Sodium 
hydroxide (strong base), the following reaction takes place:
cooH   cooNa
        +2NaoH               +2H2o
cooH   cooNa
oxalic acid  Sodium oxalate
In this titration, Phenolphthalein is used as an indicator. The 
concentration of an unknown solution is calculated in g/L. The 
molarity of the solution can be calculated by using the formula
a1 M1 V1 = a2 M2 V2 
where a1, M1, V1 are respectively the basicity, molarity and 
volume of oxalic acid used, and a2, M2 and V2 are the acidity, 
molarity and volume of NaoH, respectively, used in the titration.
The basicity of an acid is the number of replaceable H + ions 
and acidity of a base is the number of replaceable oH – ions 
from one formula unit of the substance.

theory
The following reaction takes place in this titration: 
Na2co3	+	2HCl	→	2NaCl	+	CO2 + H2o
Methyl orange is used as an indicator in this titration. The 
proton furnished by the acid neutralises Sodium carbonate 
solution. When the entire Sodium carbonate solution is 
neutralised, the next drop of the acid added produces 
the reddish orange colour, which is the end point. The 
concentration (strength) of the unknown solution is calculated 
in g/L. It is calculated from the molarity of the solution using 
the relation:
 a 1M1V1= a2M2V2
where, a1 and a2 are the acidity of the base and the basicity of 
the acid, respectively. M1 and M2 are the molarities, V1 and V2 
are the volumes of the base and the acid, respectively, used 
to neutralise each other.

redox tItratIons
The oxidation and reduction reactions involve the transfer 
of electrons from one species to another. In the oxidation 
of a substance, electrons are lost from the species and in 
reduction, electrons are gained by the species. oxidation and 
reduction reactions occur simultaneously, and therefore, 
they are known as ‘redox reactions’. Titrations involving 
redox reactions are called ‘redox titrations’. You know that in  
acid-base titrations, indicators which are sensitive to pH change 
are used to note the end point. Similarly, in redox titrations, 
there is a change in the electrode potential of the system. The 
indicators used in redox reactions are sensitive to change in 
electrode potential. The ideal oxidation-reduction indicators 
have an electrode potential intermediate between the values for 
the solution being titrated and the titrant. These values show 
sharp readily detectable colour change.

experIMent 2.5
To determine the strength/molarity of KMno 4 solution by 
titrating it against a 0.05 M standard solution of oxalic acid.
theory
In  the present experiment, Potassium permanganate acts as 
a powerful oxidising agent in acidic medium. The oxidising 
action of KMno4 in the acidic medium can be represented by 
the following equation:
Mno4
– + 8H+ + 5e–	→	Mn2+ + 4H2o
The acid used in this titration is dilute Sulphuric acid. Nitric 
acid is not used as it is an oxidising agent and Hydrochloric 
acid is usually avoided because it reacts with KMno 4, 
according to the equation given below to produce chlorine, 
which is also an oxidising agent in the aqueous solution.
2KMno4	+	16HCl	→	2KCl	+	2MnCl2 + 5cl2 + 8H2o
Since, oxalic acid acts as a reducing agent, it can be titrated 
against Potassium permanganate in the acidic medium 
involving the following reactions:
Reduction: [Mno4
– + 8H+ + 5e–	→	Mn2+ + 4H2o] × 2
oxidation: [c2o4
2–	→	2CO2 + 2e–] × 5
2Mno4
– + 5c2o4
2– + 16H+	→	2Mn2+ + 10co2 + 8H2o
In these equations, Mno 4
– is reduced to Mn 2+ and c 2o4
2– is 
oxidised to co2. The oxidation number of carbon in c2o4
2– 
changes from +3 to +4 and that of Manganese in Mno4
–
 from 
+7 to +2.
In these titrations, Potassium permanganate acts as a  
self-indicator. Initially, the colour of Potassium permanganate is 
discharged due to its reduction by oxalic acid. After the complete 
consumption of oxalate ions, the end point is indicated by the 
appearance of a light pink colour produced by the addition of 
a little excess of unreacted Potassium permanganate. Further, 
during the titration, warming oxalic acid solution (50°– 60° c) 
along with dilute H2So4 is required. This is essential because 
the reaction is very slow at higher temperature. During the 
titration, Mn2+ ions are formed, which act as a catalyst for the 
reduction of KMno4 by oxalic acid. Therefore, the heating of 
acid solution is required only in the initial stage.

Like oxalic acid, Ferrous ammonium sulphate also acts as a

Ionic equation

titration, the heating of Ferrous ammonium sulphate solution

The cations indicated by the preliminary tests given above are

preparatIon of orIgInal solutIon (os)
To prepare the original solution, follow the steps one after the 
other in a systematic order. In case, the salt does not dissolve 
in a particular solvent even on heating, try the next solvent. 
Solvents are used in the following order:

solution, thus, obtained is evaporated to dryness in a china 
dish. The residue so obtained is dissolved in distilled water.

as oS.

use of h2s In group-II and group-Iv
H2S in acidic medium is the reagent for group-II and in basic 
medium is the reagent for group-IV. For this purpose, H 2S 
gas has to be passed through the test solution. For analysis 
at macro scale, H2S gas is generated in Kipp’s apparatus and 
bubbled through the test solution. However, at microscale, 
this method is not feasible because the test tubes are small 
and	the	gas	may	push	the	solution	out.	Hence,	a	modified	
method is used for microscale analysis. A saturated solution 
of H2S is prepared in cold distilled water/cold dilute solution 
of NH4OH	in	water.	A	few	drops	of	this	solution	are	sufficient	
for the tests. This solution can be stored in a tightly stoppered 
container kept at a cool place.

the other hand, if the original solution is prepared in water  
and on the addition of dilute Hcl, a white precipitate appears, 
it may also be Pb2+. If oS is prepared in dilute Hcl, group-I

chapter 5
chroMatography
The technique of chromatography is vastly used for the 
separation,	 purification	 and	identification	 of	compounds.	
chromatography is a physical method of separation, in which 
the components to be separated are distributed between two 
phases, one of which is stationary, while the other, known as 
the	mobile	phase,	moves	in	a	definite	direction.	The	distribution	
of the component may take place either by adsorption or  
by partition.
1. adsorptIon ChroMatography
In adsorption chromatography, the substances are 
selectively adsorbed in the stationary phase. Stronger the 
adsorption, slower is the movement of the substance with 
the mobile phase. column and thin layer chromatography 
are the common examples of adsorption chromatography.
    (a) coluMn ChroMatography
In it, the stationary phase is a suitable adsorbent packed 
in a glass column. The mobile phase (a suitable solvent) 
flows down through the packed column. The weakly 
adsorbed substance is taken away by it initially, followed 
by the strongly adsorbed  substance. This results in their 
separation.
    (b) thIn layer chroMatography
The stationary phase in it is a thin layer of a suitable 
adsorbent adhering to a glass plate. The mobile phase (a 
suitable solvent) moves up due to capillary action. A weakly 
adsorbed substance moves up faster with the mobile phase 
than a strongly adsorbed substance. This results in their 
separation.
2. partItIon chroMatography
Paper chromatography is the common example of partition 
chromatography, in which water present in the pores of a

Using a particular solvent (mobile phase) and at a given

These different rates are expressed in terms of a property

To prepare Dibenzalacetone (Dibenzy-lidene acetone).
theory
The a-hydrogen atom of aliphatic aldehydes and ketones is 
acidic in nature. In the presence of dilute alkali, an aldehyde 
or ketone containing a–hydrogen condenses with an aromatic 
aldehyde to give β –unsaturated aldehyde or ketone. This 
reaction is called ‘ claisen-Schmidt reaction’. For example, 
benzaldehyde undergoes condensation with Acetone in the 
presence of aqueous Sodium hydroxide to give Dibenzalacetone.
apparatus requIred
Micro	conical	flask,	beaker	(50	mL),	funnel,	melting	point	
assembly,	thermometer	and	micro	filtration	unit.	
cheMIcals requIred
Ethanol, NaoH, Benzaldehyde, Acetone and ice.
procedure
 1. Prepare a solution of 1 g Sodium hydroxide in a mixture 
of 8 mL Ethanol and 10 mL water taken in a 50 mL 
beaker. cool the beaker in a water bath maintained at a 
temperature of about 10–15°c.
 2. Prepare a mixture of 1 mL Benzaldehyde and 0.5 mL 
Acetone	in	a	micro	conical	flask.	cool it in ice bath. Add 
half of this mixture slowly in ice cooled NaoH solution 
prepared in Step 1 with vigorous stirring. A fluffy 
precipitate is formed within 1–2 minutes. Stir the mixture 
gently	for	about	five	minutes.
 3. After five minutes, add the remaining mixture  
of Benzaldehyde and Acetone and occasionally stir for 
30 minutes.
 4. Filter the pale yellow solid obtained and wash with  
cold water. Dry it and crystallise its small amount  
using alcohol.

text:
chapter 8
surface cheMIstry
In a true solution, solute particles mix homogeneously with 
the molecules of a solvent, and thus, form a single phase. 
However, a colloidal solution is a heterogeneous system, 
in which very fine particles of one substance disperse 
(dispersed phase) in another substance called dispersion 
medium. Particles of the dispersed phase do not form a 
single phase with particles of the dispersion medium as they 
are either very large molecules or essentially aggregates of 
small molecules. colloidal particles are larger in size than 
simple molecules but small enough to remain suspended 
in the dispersion medium (1–100 nm). Some examples of 
very large molecules which form colloidal dispersion are 
starch, gum and proteins, whereas, colloidal Sulphur is 
an example of aggregate of small molecules. Further, a 
heterogeneous system of a solid as dispersed phase and 
a liquid as dispersion medium is called a ‘sol’. Depending 
upon the nature of interaction between the dispersed phase 
and the dispersion medium, colloidal sols are divided into 
two categories, namely, lyophilic (solvent attracting) and 
lyophobic (solvent repelling). If water is the dispersion 
medium, the terms used are ‘hydrophilic’ and ‘hydrophobic’. 
Egg albumin, starch and gum are lyophilic sols. Freshly 
prepared Ferric hydroxide, Aluminium hydroxide and Arsenic 
sulphide sols are examples of lyophobic sols. A few methods 
of preparation of colloids are — chemical methods, electrical 
disintegration, mechanical methods, like grinding, use of a 
colloid mill and peptisation. In this unit, you will learn to 
prepare both types of sols. Also, you will learn a method for 
purification	of	sols.

text:
Surface chemiStry
107
experIMent 8.3
To study the role of emulsifying agents in stabilising the 
emulsion of different oils.
theory
Emulsion is a type of colloid, in which both the dispersed phase 
and the dispersion medium are liquids. Here, the ‘dispersed 
phase’ and the ‘dispersion medium’ are distinguished by 
their relative amounts. The one, which is present in smaller 
proportion, is called ‘dispersed phase’, while the other, 
which is present in relatively large quantity, is known as the 
‘dispersion medium’.
When oil is shaken with water, a faint milky mixture is often 
observed, which is unstable and is called an emulsion of oil in 
water (o/w). on standing, it gets separated into two layers, i.e., 
oil and water. The mixing capacity of different oils with water 
is different. This mixing capacity of an oil, in addition to its 
nature, depends on the method of shaking also (i.e., vigorous 
shaking or swirling). The stability of an oil in water emulsion 
is increased by the addition of a suitable emulsifying agent, 
such as soap solution. Soap contains Sodium salt of long 
chain Aliphatic carboxylic acids with carboxyl group as the 
polar group, which decreases the inter-facial tension between 
oil and water. Hence, oil mixes with water in greater quantity 
and	emulsification	takes	place.	The	minimum	concentration	
of	soap	required	for	complete	emulsification	is	called	‘optimum	
concentration’. Any other amount, less or more than this 
optimum amount, does not cause effective stablisation.
apparatus requIred
Six	test	tubes,	five	droppers,	test	tube	stand,	one	glass	rod	
and one stopwatch.
cheMIcals requIred
Soap/detergent — 0.1g, mustard oil, linseed oil, castor oil and 
machine oil — 1 mL each.

text:
chapter 9
cheMIcal KInetIcs
chemical kinetics is the study of the rates of the chemical 
reactions and the factors which affect these rates.
rate of reactIon
Rate of reaction can be measured in terms of either decrease 
in concentration of any one of the reactants or increase in 
concentration of any one of the products with time.
Factors, such as concentration, temperature and catalyst 
affect the rate of reaction.
Sodium thiosulphate reacts with Hydrochloric acid and 
produces a colloidal solution of Sulphur, which makes the 
solution translucent. The reaction occurs as follows:
Na2S2o3(aq)	+	2HCl(aq)	→	2NaCl(aq)	+	H2o(l) + So2(g) + S(s)
Ionic form of the above reaction is written as:
S2o3
2_
 (aq) + 2H+	(aq)	→H2o(l) + So2(g) + S(s)
The property of the colloidal solution of Sulphur to make the 
solution translucent is used to study the rate of precipitation 
of Sulphur. The rate of precipitation of Sulphur increases 
with an increase in the concentration of the reacting species 
or with an increase in the temperature of the system. With 
an increase in the concentration of reactants, the number of 
molecular collisions per unit time between the reacting species 
increases and consequently, the chances of product formation 
increase. This results in an increase in the rate of precipitation 
of Sulphur. Similarly, on increasing the temperature, the 
kinetic energy of the reacting species increases, so the number 
of effective collisions that result in the formation of products 
increase leading to a faster rate of reaction.

The reaction between Iodide ions and Hydrogen peroxide 
occurs in the acidic medium and can be represented in the 
following manner:
2I
–
(aq) + H2o2(aq) + 2H+(aq)	→	I2(aq) + 2H2o(l)

molecular Iodine. If calculated amount of Sodium thiosulphate

2–(aq) + 2I–(aq)

text:
chapter 10
therMocheMIstry
Most of the reactions are carried out at atmospheric pressure, 
which remains nearly constant. Heat changes measured for 
reactions carried out under a constant pressure (which may 
or may not be equal to the atmospheric pressure) are enthalpy 
changes. Enthalpy changes are directly related to temperature 
changes by the relation:
										∆H		=	 qp
                 = M.cp.	∆T	 	 			............	(1)
Where, m = Mass
           cp		 =	 Specific	heat	capacity	at	constant	pressure
										∆T		 =	 Change	in	temperature
Measurement of heat changes is generally carried out in 
metallic vessels called ‘calorimeters’. Metallic calorimeters 
are not used for studying thermochemical changes because 
metals may react with the substances used. Stainless steel or  
gold-plated copper calorimeters may be used. Reactions may 
also	be	carried	out	in	glass	beakers	placed	in	thermos	flask	
or in a thermally-insulated box or in a styrofoam cup.
During the measurement of heat changes, calorimeter, 
thermometer and stirrer also absorb some heat. This amount 
of heat should also be known. It may be calculated from the 
heat capacity of calorimeter c, which may be determined 
experimentally. In case of a glass vessel (e.g., beaker), the 
heat capacity for that part of the beaker, which is actually in 
contact with the reaction mixture, is found. This is so because 
the thermal conductivity of glass is low and only the area of 
glass vessel in contact with the liquid absorbs the maximum 
heat. The heat capacity of the calorimeter, therefore, varies 
with the volume of the liquid taken in it.

Method of mixtures is used to determine the heat capacity of 
calorimeter. For this purpose, a known volume of hot water 
at a known temperature is added to a known volume of water 
contained in the calorimeter at room temperature. Since 
energy is conserved, the heat gained by the calorimeter and 
cold water should be equal to the heat lost by the hot water. 
Thus, we can write the following equation:
Heat gained by cold water and calorimeter = Heat lost by  
hot water
c(tm–tc)+ mccp(tm–tc) = mh cp(th–tm) (2).

the mixture, respectively

cp	=	Specific	heat	capacity	of	water
mc and mh = Masses of the cold and hot water, respectively

For water, cp = 4.184 J ◦c–1 g–1

experIMent 10.1
To determine the enthalpy of the solution of Potassium nitrate 
(1:200 molar ratio).
theory
Solution formation is often accompanied by enthalpy change. 
Enthalpy of a solution is the amount of heat liberated or 
absorbed	when	one	mole	of	a	solute	is	dissolved	in	a	specified	
amount of solvent (usually water) under a constant pressure. 
The amount of solvent (water) is expressed in terms of its 
number of moles (n). The ratio of the amount of solute and 
solvent is expressed as 1:n. For example, the ratio 1:200 
means that 1 mole solute is dissolved in 200 mole solvent.
apparatus requIred 
calorimeter (50 mL beaker inserted in LDPE foam case), digital 
thermometer (0.1°c), stirrer (glass), beaker (50 mL), tripod

procedure

 1. Take a beaker of 50 mL capacity. clean and dry it. To

 2. Place the beaker in an LDPE foam case. Insert the stirrer 
and thermometer in the lid. Adjust the position of the 
thermometer in a way that it passes through the loop of 
the	stirrer.	Adjust	the	height	of	the	thermometer	to	fit	
the case.
 3. Record the temperature of water in the calorimeter and 
check after two minutes for its constant value. Let it be tc.

water and rinse it. Add 10 mL distilled water with the 
help of a 5 mL pipette.
 5. Heat the above beaker on a wire gauge placed on a 
tripod stand by 10°c as compared to the water in the 
calorimeter.

chapter 11

experIMent 11.1
To study the variation of cell potential of the cell Zn |Zn2+||cu2+| 
cu with change in the concentration of electrolytes at room 
temperature.
theory
The potential difference between two electrodes of a galvanic 
cell is called ‘cell potential’ and is measured in volts. It is the 
difference between the electrode potentials of cathode and 
anode. When no current is drawn from the cell, it is called 
electromotive force (emf) of the cell.
      Ecell = Ecathode –    Eanode                     (1)
The potential of individual half-cells cannot be measured.  
We can measure the emf of a cell that gives the difference 
between two half-cell potentials. According to the International 
Union of Applied chemistry (IUPAc) convention, standard 
Hydrogen electrode represented by Pt, H2 (g, 1 bar)/H+(aq, 1M) 
is assigned zero potential at all temperatures corresponding 
to the reaction.
H+(aq) + e–	→		1 H2(g)
                      2
Half-cell potentials are measured with respect to standard 
hydrogen electrode. A cell is constructed by taking standard 
hydrogen electrode as anode (reference half-cell) and the other 
electrode, under standard condition, of which the electrode 
potential is to be measured as cathode. Then, the cell potential 
is equal to the standard electrode potential of the other half-cell.
E°cell = E°cathode –   E°anode
       =  E°cathode
                                                    because E°anode = 0

text:
The National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) has already 
developed Science and Mathematics Kits for upper primary and secondary 
stages and Micro Scale Chemistry Kit for higher secondary stage in its endeavour 
to support teaching and learning in schools by inculcating process skills of 
science. These kits have been well received in States and schools. Over the 
years, need has been expressed by different stakeholders in schools for a kit 
at the higher secondary stage in physics. Improvising the apparatuses used 
in traditional physics laboratories and developing low cost items which can 
fit in a portable box was indeed a challenging task. But with dedicated and 
sustained effort of the Division, we have finally succeeded in designing and 
developing such a kit. 
This kit is primarily meant for schools where either a functional laboratory 
does not exist or a lab does not have proper instruments. Most of the experiments 
and activities prescribed in the NCERT syllabus of Physics for higher secondary 
classes can be performed by using this kit. Work is in progress for improvising 
some more items like Searle’s apparatus and Travelling microscope and we 
hope that soon these items will also find place in the physics laboratory kit. 
Even in absence of these items, a student can perform the required number of 
experiments, given the option available in the list of prescribed experiments.
This kit will facilitate practical work in our rural schools also which usually 
lack proper physics laboratory and necessary equipments. Experiments are 
the key component of any science curriculum, but in practice it has been 
observed that most of our rural schools and even some urban schools are not 
properly equipped with the laboratory facilities required at higher secondary 
stage. This endeavour may give a plausible solution to this basic problem and 
can encourage teachers and  students to do science in a manner it is expected.
We hope that design of some of the items of this kit will inspire teachers 
and students to think of alternative design/methods for performing a particular 
experiment by using local resources. In addition to the experiments given in 
the list, many more experiments can be carried out using the same kit items.
The advantage of this kit is that it is portable and therefore it can be carried 
into the classrooms and can also be used for demonstration purposes. 
In this kit we have modified/improvised/customised many of the instruments 
required in performing experiments at higher secondary stage.
Some of the examples are:
• Improvised optical bench — In traditional labs optical benches are bulky 
and costly, but we have improvised optical bench which is small in size 
and light in weight so that it can be moved easily from one place to other. 
• Improvised meter bridge — Total length of this device, traditionally, is more 
than one metre, therefore we have made it in two halves that can be joined 
with the help of a jointer.
• Small size potentiometer — Normally the length of this device is also more 
than one metre, but we have improvised it by designing it on approximately 
half metre board.

• Improvised apparatus for verification of Boyle’s law — In place of costly and 
sophisticated apparatus used in traditional lab for this purpose we have 
improvised it with the help of simple syringe and wooden blocks.
• Improvised apparatus for resonance of sound — We have used a tube which 
can also be used in another experiment for finding coefficient of viscosity 
of liquids, and in this way reduce the cost and space. 
• Diode and transistor characteristic apparatus — Traditional laboratories 
use costly setup for semiconductor experiments but we have developed low 
cost power supplies fitted in a box and provided with a breadboard .With 
the help of these not only the experiments mentioned in the manual but 
also many other experiments can be performed.
We have improvised many other items like sonometer, resistance box, pan 
balance, etc.
No attempt has been made to improvise some of the items like vernier 
callipers, screw gauge, and spherometer. Because firstly we don’t want to 
compromise with precision of the measurements made by these devices and 
secondly, these items are neither bulky nor costly and  are easily available in 
school labs.
This manual consists of two parts — The first part covers the experiments 
and activities for Class–XI and the second part the experiments and activities 
for Class-XII. Most of the experiments have been presented under the following 
subheadings — Aim, Apparatus and Material Required, Description of 
Apparatus, Formula Used, Procedure, Observations and Calculation, Result, 
Precautions and Sources of Error.
We have adopted/adapted some part of Laboratory Manual in Physics 
for Classes XI–XII developed by NCERT during 2010. We acknowledge the 
contribution of members of development team of the manual in Physics.
Each of the experiments and activities suggested in this kit has gone 
through a series of try-outs, modification before finalisation. We are grateful to 
the teachers and subject experts from different institutions who participated 
in the workshops organised for the development, review and refinement of the 
kit items and kit manual.
I acknowledge the valuable contributions of V.P. Srivastava, former 
Professor of Physics and other team members who contributed and helped in 
the development of the higher secondary Physics Kit and Kit Manual. Special 
thanks are due to Ashish Kumar Srivastava, Coordinator of this programme 
for his dedicated and valuable contribution in the development of this kit and 
kit manual.
We warmly welcome comments and suggestions from our valued users for 
further improvement of this Kit and Kit Manual.
R.K. PaRashaR

Aim
To determine the radius of curvature of a given spherical surface

AppArAtus And mAteriAl required
A spherometer, a spherical surface such as a watch glass or a convex 
mirror	and	a	plane	glass	plate	of	about	6	cm	×	6	cm	size.
prinCiple
Pitch: It	is	the	vertical	distance	moved	by	the	central	screw	in	one	
complete rotation of the circular disc scale.
Commonly used spherometers in school laboratories have 
graduations	in	millimetres	on	the	main	scale	and	may	have100	equal	
divisions	on	circular	disc	scale.	In	one	rotation	of	the	circular	scale,	
the central screw advances or recedes by 1 mm. Thus, the pitch of 
the screw is 1 mm.
Least Count: Least count of a spherometer is the distance moved 
by the spherometer screw when it is turned through one division 
on the circular scale, i.e., least count of the spherometer =  
Pitch of the spherometer screw
Numb erofdivisionsonthecirculaarscale
The least count of commonly used 
spherometers is 0.01 mm. 
However, some spherometers have 
least count as small as 0.005 mm or 
0.001 mm.

desCriptiOn OF physiCAl BAlAnCe
A beam balance is a device that measures the gravitational mass of 
an object by comparing it with a standard gravitational mass. 
 The most commonly used two-pan beam balance is an application of 
a	lever.	It	consists	of	a	rigid	uniform	bar	(beam),	two	pans	suspended	
from each end, and a pivotal point in the centre of the bar (Fig. E 
4.1). At this pivotal point, a support (called fulcrum) is set at right 
angles to the beam. This beam balance works on the principle of 
moments. An improvised beam 
balance is shown in Fig. E 4.1.
If	an	object	having	gravitational	
mass m is placed on one pan 
of the beam balance and a 
standard mass of known value 
m1 is placed on the other pan of 
the balance, then according to 
the principle of moments:
 mg x1 = m1g x2, 
If,	
x1=x2=x  then, m=m1
As m1 is known, it becomes 
possible for us to known m.Fig. E 4.1: A beam balance and set of weights

Measurement of the weight of a given body (a wooden block) using 
the parallelogram law of vector addition.
AppArAtus And mAteriAl required
The given body with hook, the parallelogram law of vector apparatus 
(improvised Gravesand’s apparatus), strong thread, slotted weights 
(two sets), white paper, thin mirror strip and sharp pencil.
FOrmulA used
Let	P	and	Q	be	the	magnitudes	of	the	two	forces	and	θ	the	angle	
between them. Then the resultant R of P and Q is given by 
R= P+  Q +2PQcos2 2 θ
If	two	known	forces	P	and	Q	and	a	third	unknown	force	R	due	to	the	
weight of the given body are made to act at a point O [Fig. E 5.1 (a)] 
such	that	they	are	in	equilibrium,	then	the	unknown	force	is	equal	
to the resultant of the two forces. Thus, the weight of a given body 
can be determined.

1.  Set the top cover of kit box in vertical position by using two 
rods provided in the kit. Fix the pulleys P1 and P2 at two edges 
of the top cover with s-clamp. Ensure that the pulleys are 
moving smoothly. This is actually our improvised Gravesand's 
apparatus. Fix a sheet of white paper on the wooden top cover 
of the kit box with drawing pins.
2.		 Take	a	sufficiently	long	piece	of	string	and	tie	the	two	hangers	
at its ends. Tie another shorter string in the midpoint O of the 
first	string.	Tie	the	given	body	of	unknown	weight	at	the	other	
end of the shorter string. Arrange them on the pulley as shown 
in	Fig.	E	5.1	(a)	with	slotted	weights	on	the	hangers.	Improvised	
Gravesand’s apparatus is now ready for use.
3.  Add weights in the hangers such that the junction of the threads 
is	in	equilibrium	in	the	lower	half	of	the	paper.	Make	sure	that	
neither the weights nor the threads touch the board or the table.
4.  First step is to bring the knot of the threads to position of  
no-friction.	For	this,	first	bring	the	knot	to	a	point	on	extreme	
right or left of its position. On leaving there, it moves towards the 
position	of	no-friction	because	it	is	not	in	equilibrium.	While	it	so	
moves, tap the board gently. The point where the knot ultimately 
comes to rest is taken as the position of no-friction; mark this 
with a point. Repeat the procedure several times. Each time let 
the knot approach the position of no-friction from a different 
direction and mark the point where it comes to rest. Find by 
judgment the centre of those points which are close together. 
Mark this centre as O.
5.  To mark the direction of the force acting along a string, place a 
mirror strip below the string on the paper. Adjust the position of 
the eye such that there is no parallax between the string and its 
image. Mark the two points A1 and A2 at the edges of the mirror 
where the image of the string leaves the mirror [Fig. E 5.1 (b)].
  Similarly, mark the directions of other two strings, that is forces, 
by	points	B1	and	B2 and by points X1 and X2 along the strings 
OB	and	OX	respectively.
6.  Remove the hangers and note the weight of each hanger and 
slotted weights on them.
7.		 Remove	the	paper	from	the	board	and	place	it	flat	on	the	
table. Join the three pairs of points marked on the paper and 
extend these lines to meet at O. These three lines represent the 
directions of the three forces.

AIM
Plot L – T and L – T2 graphs for a simple pendulum and to find the 
effective length of second’s pendulum using appropriate graph.
APPARATus ANd MATERIAl REquIREd
Clamp stand; a split cork; a heavy metallic (brass/iron) spherical bob 
with a hook; a long, fine and strong cotton thread or string (about  
2.0 m); stopwatch; metre scale, graph paper, pencil and eraser.
PROCEduRE
1. Place the clamp stand on the table. Tie the hook attached to 
the pendulum bob to one end of the string of about 150 cm in 
length.  Pass the other end of the string through two half-pieces 
of a split cork.
2. Clamp the split cork firmly in the clamp 
stand so that the pendulum hangs 
vertically [FigE 6.1]. Mark with a piece 
of chalk or ink, the point just below 
where the bob is at rest (called as mean 
position). Draw a straight line through 
this point along the plane of oscillation 
of the pendulum. Take care that the 
pendulum hangs vertically (about 2 cm 
above the floor) beyond the edge of the 
table so that it is free to oscillate.
3. Measure the length l of the string between 
the point of suspension and the top of the 
hook of simple pendulum.
4. Displace the bob to one side along the 
line drawn below it. Make sure that the 
angular displacement of the bob is not more than 15 degrees, 
from the vertical position OA and then release it gently. In case 
you find that the stand is shaky, put some heavy object on its

5. Keep the pendulum oscillating for some time.  After completion 
of 3–5 oscillations, start the stop-watch/clock as the pendulum 
bob just crosses its mean position (say, from left to right). Count 
it as zero oscillation.
6. Keep on counting oscillations 1,2,3,…, n, everytime the bob

mean of these readings. Compute the time for one oscillation, 
i.e., the time period T ( = t/n) of the pendulum.
7. Change the length of the pendulum, by about 10 cm. Repeat 
the Step 6 again for finding the time (t) for about 20 oscillations 
or more for the new length and find the mean time period. Take 
5 or 6 more observations for different lengths of pendulum and 
find mean time period in each case.
8. Record observations in the tabular form with proper units  
(Table E 6.1). 
9. Take effective length L along x-axis and T 2 (or T) along y-axis,

Aim
To determine the speed of sound in air at room temperature using 
a resonance tube.
AppArAtus And mAteriAl required
Resonance tube assembly (improvised), a tuning fork of known 
frequency (preferably of 512 Hz), a rubber pad, a thermometer, two 
laboratory stands with clamps and water.
FormulA used
The speed of sound in air at room temperature would 
be v = 2n(l2 – l1).
Where l1 is length of air column at first resonance and 
l2 is the length of air column at second resonance. n is 
the frequency of the tuning fork.
procedure
Setting up of improvised resonance tube
1. To set up the improvised resonance tube, following  
 materials have been provided in the kit:
(a) A 60 cm long tube of diameter about 5 cm with 
a centimetre scale fixed on it to be used as a 
resonance tube.
(b) A plastic bottle without its bottom to be used 
as a reservoir.

at its two ends. One of the rubber stoppers is to be filled 
into tube while the other is to be fixed at the mouth of the 
plastic tube.
(d) Two laboratory stands with clamps to fix the tube and the 
bottle.
2. Fix the rubber stopper at that end of the resonance tube where 
the scale reads 60 cm. Fix the other stopper to the mouth of 
the plastic bottle (reservoir).
3. Fix the resonance tube vertically using a laboratory stand. 
Similarly, fix the reservoir vertically using another laboratory 
stand. Take care that the reservoir is fixed with its open end 
at the highest point of the laboratory stand. Ensure that the 
resonance tube and the reservoir are vertical (Fig. E 14.1).
4. Note the room temperature with a thermometer. Also, note the 
frequency ν of the given tuning fork.
Determination of First Resonance Position
5. Fill the water in the reservoir such that the level of water in 
the resonance tube reaches up to its open end. Make sure that 
there is no leakage of water from the resonance tube and the 
reservoir.
6. Close the pinch cock and lower down the position of reservoir 
on the vertical rod.
7. Gently strike the given tuning fork on a rubber pad and put it 
nearly 1 cm above the open end of the resonance tube. Keep both 
the prongs of the tuning fork parallel to the ground and lying 
one above the other so that the prongs vibrate in the vertical 
plane. Try to listen the sound being produced in the tube. It 
may not be audible in this position.
8. Slowly loosen the pinch cock to let the water level fall in the 
resonance tube very slowly. Keep bringing the tuning fork 
near the open end of the resonance tube, notice the increasing 
loudness of the sound.
9. Repeat Steps 7 and 8 till you get the exact position of water level 
in the tube for which the intensity of sound being produced in 
the tube is maximum. This corresponds to the first resonance 
position or fundamental note, if the length of air column is 
minimum. Close the pinch cock at this position and note the 
position of water level or length l 1 of  air column in the tube. 
This is the determination of first resonance position while the 
level of water is falling in the tube.
10. Repeat Steps 5 to 9 to confirm the first resonance position.

Aim
 To determine the specific heat capacity of a given (i) solid and  
(ii) liquid by the method of mixtures.
AppArAtus And mAteriAl required
Copper calorimeter with lid, stirrer and insulating cover, two 
thermometers (0 °C to 110 °C, with a least count of 0.5 °C), a solid 
(pendulum bob), given liquid, two beakers (100 mL and 250 mL), a 
heating device (heater/hot plate/gas burner); physical balance with 
weight box (including fractional weights or spring balance), a piece of 
strong non-flexible thread (25–30 cm long), water, laboratory stand, 
tripod stand and wire gauze.
principle
For a body of mass m and specific heat capacity s, the amount of 
heat Q lost/gained by it when its temperature falls/rises is given by
    DQ = ms Dt             (E 15.1)
Specific heat capacity: It is the amount of heat required to raise 
the temperature of unit mass of a substance through 1°C. Its S.I. 
unit is Jkg–1K–1.
Principle of Calorimetry: If bodies of different temperatures are 
brought in thermal contact, at thermal equilibrium the amount of 
heat lost by the body at higher temperature is equal to the amount 
of heat gained by the body at lower temperature, provided no heat 
is lost to the surrounding.
  (i) Specific heat capacity of given solid by method of mixtures
procedure
1. Set the physical balance and make sure that all initial adjustments 
are made.

Aim
To determine the mass of a given body using a metre scale by the 
principle of moments.
AppArAtus And mAteriAl required
A wooden metre scale of uniform thickness (a wooden strip of one 
metre length having uniform thickness and width can also be used); 
load of unknown mass, wooden or metal wedge with sharp edge, 
weight box, thread (nearly 30 cm long), a spirit level, and a raised 
platform of about 20 cm height (such as a wooden or metal block).
principle
For a body in equilibrium, which is free to rotate about a fixed 
axis, the sum of the clockwise moments is equal to the sum of the 
anticlockwise moments.
If  M 1 is the known mass, suspended at a distance l1 on one side 
from the centre of gravity of a beam and M2 is the unknown mass, 
suspended at a distance l2 on the other side from the centre of gravity, 
and the beam is in equilibrium, then M2 l2 = M1 l1.
procedure
1. Make a raised platform on a table. One can use a wooden or a 
metal block or a pile of books. However, the platform should be 
sturdy. Place a wedge having a sharp edge on it.
2. Make two loops of thread to be used for suspending the unknown 
mass and the weights from the metre scale (beam). Insert the 
loops at about 10 cm from the edge of the metre scale from both 
sides.
3. Place the metre scale with thread loops on the wedge and adjust 
it till it is balanced. Mark two points on the scale above the 
wedge where the scale is balanced. Join these two points with 
a straight line which would facilitate to pin point the location of

text:
Aim
To plot a graph for a given set of data choosing proper scale and 
show error bars due to the precision of the instruments.
AppArAtus And mAteriAl required
Graph paper, a pencil, a scale and a set of data.
principle
Any measurement using a device has an uncertainty in its value 
depending on the precision of the device used. For example, in the 
measurement of diameter of a spherical bob, the correct way is to 
represent it d + ∆d, where ∆d is the uncertainty in measurement 
of d given by the least count of the vernier/screw gauze used. 
Representation of d + ∆d in a graph is shown as a line having a 
length of + ∆d about point ‘d’. This is known as the error bar of d.
Here, we consider the uncertainty in measurements only due to 
the least count of the measuring instrument so as to learn how 
uncertainty for a given data is shown in a line graph.
Let us take the example of the graph between time period T, and the 
length l, of a simple pendulum. The uncertainty in measurement 
of time period will depend on the least count of the stopwatch/
clock, while that the measurement of length of the pendulum will 
depend on the least count of the device(s) used to measure length.  
Table A 3.1 gives the data for the time period of simple pendulum 
measured in an experiment along with the uncertainty in the 
measurement of the length and time period of the pendulum.
plottinG oF A GrApH WitH error BArs
Steps involved in drawing a graph with error bars on it are as follows:
1. Draw x and y axes on a graph sheet and select an appropriate 
scale for plotting of the graph. In order to show uncertainty/error 
in given data, it is advisable that the scale chosen should be such 
that the lowest value of uncertainty/error on either axis could 
be shown by at least the smallest division on the graph sheet.

Aim
To study the variation in the range of a jet of water with the change 
in the angle of projection.
AppArAtus And mAteriAl required
PVC or rubber pipe, a nozzle, source of water under pressure (i.e., 
a tap connected to an overhead water tank or water supply line), a 
measuring tape and a large size protractor.
procedure
1. Making a large protractor: Take a circular plyboard or thick 
circular cardboard sheet of radius about 25 cm. Draw a 
diameter through its centre. Cut it along with the diameter to 
form two D′s. On one of the dees, draw angles at an interval of 
15° starting from 0°.
2. Attach one end of pipe to a tap. At the other end of the pipe fix 
a nozzle to obtain a jet of water. Ensure that there is no leakage 
in the pipe.
3. Fix the graduated D vertically on the ground with its graduated–
face towards you, as shown in Fig. A 5.1.
4. Place the nozzle at the centre O of the protractor and direct the 
nozzle along θ =15° mark.
5. Open the tap to obtain a jet of water. Ensure that water leaves 
the nozzle at an angle of 15° from the horizontal and also the 
ground in front is in level with point O and horizontal. The water 
coming out of the jet would strike the ground after completing 
its parabolic trajectory. Ask your friend to mark the point (A) 
where the water falls. Close the tap.
6. Measure the distance between point O and A. This gives the 
range R corresponding to the angle of projection, 15°.

Activity6
Aim
To study the conservation of energy of a ball rolling down an inclined 
plane (using a curved channel or a transparent flexible tube).
AppArAtus And mAteriAl required
A curved channel (radius of curvature 30–35 cm, length 65 cm) 
made of a strong metal, or transparent flexible tube, a steel ball of 
about 1.5 cm diameter, spirit level, tissue paper or cotton, laboratory 
stand, clamp and a half metre scale.
principle
The law of conservation of energy states that ‘energy can neither be 
created nor destroyed but can only be changed from one form to 
another’.
For a mechanical system, viz., the rolling of a steel ball on a perfectly 
smooth channel, the energy of ball remains in the form of its kinetic 
and potential energies and during the course of motion, a continuous 
Fig.A 6.1:  Set up for studying the conservation of energy 
using transparent flexible tube
edition:
First Edition

Reprinted Edition   
January 2019  Pausha 1940
March 2020  Phalguna 1941

text:
Activity 6
77
transformation between these energies takes place. The sum of its 
kinetic and potential energies remains constant provided there is no 
dissipation of energy due to air resistance, friction etc.
In this experiment, the law of conservation of energy is illustrated 
by the motion of a steel ball rolling in a transparent flexible tube.
When the ball is released from point A on one end of the tube, it will 
roll down inside the tube and go up on the opposite side to point B, 
about the same height h from which it was released. If the radius of 
the curved tube on right hand side is changed, the ball will still move 
till it reaches the same vertical height from which it was released.
At point A, the steel ball possesses only potential energy and zero 
kinetic energy. The potential energy transforms into kinetic energy 
when it settles down to the bottom of the tube (Q). As the ball starts 
rolling up towards point B, the kinetic energy is converted back 
into potential energy and when the ball stops at point B, it has only 
potential energy and zero kinetic energy. The law of conservation 
of mechanical energy can be verified by the equality of two vertical 
heights AA′ and BB′. Due to the loss of energy against friction, BB′ 
will always be slightly samller than AA′.
procedure
1. Adjust the experimental table horizontally with the help of spirit 
level.
2. Clean the steel ball and the flexible tube with cotton or tissue 
paper. Even a minute amount of dust or stain on the ball or in 
the tube can cause much friction.
3. Set the curved tube vertically on a horizontal table with the help 
of clamp stands.
4. Release the steel ball from point A of the curved tube. Find the 
vertical height AA′ (h) of the point A from the table using a scale.
5. Note the point B up to which the ball reaches the tube on the 
other side when the ball was released from point A. Find the 
vertical height BB′ (h′) (Fig. A. 6.1). Record the observations. 
While observing the highest position of the steel ball on other 
side, observer has to be very alert as the ball stays at the highest 
position only for an instant.
6. Repeat the activity for different initial heights of the same tube 
and note the heighest position to which the steel ball rolls up 
on other side of the tube in each case. Record the observation 
in the Table A 6.1.

2. Both halves of the tube must lie in the same vertical plane.

PRECAUTIONS
1. Ensure that there are no kinks and the wire is taut.
2. All the connections and plugs should be tight.
3. Jockey should be moved gently over the metre bridge wire.
4. The plug in the key (K) should be inserted only at the time of 
taking observations.
5. Balance points should be in the middle of the wire (30 cm to  
70 cm)
6. Initially a thick copper wire across the terminals of the 
galvanometer may be used as shunt while determining the balance 
point. However, shunt should be removed while determining the 
exact balance point.
7. Open the plug key when not measuring any reading to prevent 
unnecessary battery drains.
SOURCES OF ERROR
1. The metre bridge wire may not be of uniform area of cross-section.
2. Effect of end resistances due to metallic strips and connecting 
screws, may affect the measurement.
3. The length L of the wire should not include the lengths below the 
terminals when placed in gap E or F.
4. The resistances of end pieces/metal strips may not be negligible. 
The error introduced by it can be reduced by interchanging the 
known and unknown resistances in gaps E and F.
5. The length measurements may have error if the metre bridge wire 
is not taut and along the scale in the metre bridge.
6 Galvanometer pointer is expected to be at zero when no current 
flows through it. However, many times it is observed that it is not 
so. In such cases, pointer has to be adjusted to zero by gently 
moving the screw below the scale with the help of a screw driver. 
If it is not possible to adjust the pointer, the balance point should 
be considered at the point at which tapping of the jockey does 
not show any deflection in the galvanometer.

APPARATUS AND MATERIAL REQUIRED

PRINCIPLE
Galvanometer
Galvanometer is a sensitive device used to detect very low current. 
Its working is based on the principle that a coil placed in a uniform 
magnetic field experiences a torque when an electric current is set 
up in it. The deflection of the coil is determined by a pointer attached 
to it, moving on the scale.

AIM
To find image distance (v) for different values of object distance (u) 
for a given concave mirror and to calculate its focal length.
APPARATUS AND MATERIAL REQUIRED
Improvised optical bench assembly, two sharp-edged needles (pencils 
of two different colours with sharp tip), concave mirror of less than 
20 cm focal length, three uprights (with sliding bases), a ground 
glass screen and spirit level.
PROCEDURE
1. Determination of rough focal length 
 Determine the rough focal length of the given concave mirror. 
For this you will require the concave mirror, screen and a scale.
(i) Stand in shade facing a brightly lit distant object. The distant 
object could be a building, tree or any other object in sun 
light.
(ii) Hold the mirror in your one hand and screen in the other 
hand. Point the mirror towards the selected object and place 
the screen in front of the mirror.
 Move the mirror in forward or backward direction till you obtain 
a sharp image of the selected object on the screen. You may 
have to tilt the mirror to get the image on the screen.
 Measure the distance between the mirror and screen. This will 
give you the rough focal length of the concave mirror. 
2. Set up the optical bench as explained in Appendix 1. Make sure 
that the bench is horizontal (levelled).
3. Removing parallax 
 To understand what is parallax, do the following activity. Stretch 
index finger of one hand in vertical position and place the index

Move your head to left and then to right while keeping your eyes 
on the tip of the two fingers. What do you observe? Do you find 
both fingers moving together whether you move your head to 
the left or to the right? 
 Now, place one of the index fingers behind the other such that 
there is a gap of 5–6 cm between them. Move your head from one 
side to the other while observing the two fingers. Do you notice 
that the nearby finger changes its position with respect to the 
second finger as you move your head from one side to the other. 
We say that there is a parallax between the two fingers when 
they are not coinciding with each other. In the earlier case when 
one finger was placed just above the other, i.e., there was no 
parallax between them the two fingers appeared to move together 
when you moved your head, so we can locate the position of the 
real image of an object by just bringing another similar object 
as close to it as possible so that no parallax appears between 
the two.
4. Optical Alignment

(ii) Adjust the height of the object and image (pencil tips) to

PROCEDURE
1. Determine the rough focal length f, of the given convex lens 
following the steps suggested for concave mirror in Experiment 9.

on the screen measure the distance between the lens and the

colours on left and right hand sides of the lens respectively.

become equal to the height of the optical centre O of the lens.

AIM
To study the effect of intensity of light (by varying distance of the 
source) on a LDR (Light Dependent Resistor).
APPARATUS AND MATERIAL REQUIRED
LDR, torch, metre scale, multimeter and laboratory stand.
PRINCIPLE
Light dependent resistor or a photoresistor is a device that is sensitive 
to light. Its resistance varies according to the intensity of light 
incident on it. It is made from a semiconductor 
material with light resistors to have light 
sensitive properties, one such material is, 
cadmium sulphide. Snake-like coils are made 
of cadmium sulphide on thin metal films (Fig. 
A 7.1). LDR has a high resistance due to the 
fact that majority of electrons are locked into 
the crystal lattices and not free to move. As 
light falls on the lattice, some of the electrons 
get sufficient energy to break free the crystal 
lattice to conduct electricity. A typical LDR has 
resistance of 1 MΩ in total darkness and a few 
hundred ohm resistance in bright light.
Fig. A 7.1:  A Light Dependent 
Resistance (LDR)
PROCEDURE
1. Set up a torch on a fixed stand in vertical position facing LDR. 
Adjust LDR normally below the lamp at about 10cm (say).
2. Observe the reading of resistance using multimeter.
3. Changing the distance between torch or lamp and LDR by 15cm 
(say), repeat Step1. Record your observation and calculate 
resistance of LDR at different distances of the torch.

PRINCIPLE
1. A diode (p-n junction) is a two terminal device. It conducts when 
forward biased and does not conduct when reverse biased. The 
side having a silver band is n-side and the other side is p-side 
[Fig. 8.1a].
2. A LED (light emitting diode) is a p-n junction diode that emits 
light. It is also a two terminal device. It conducts when forward 
biased and does not conduct when reverse biased [Fig. 8.1b]. 
The long pin is connected from p-side and short pin from n-side.
3. A transistor is a three terminal semiconductor device. The 
terminals represent emitter (E), base (B) and collector (C) [Fig. 8.1c].
4. An IC (integrated circuit) is a multi-terminal device in the form 
of a chip [Fig. 8.1d].
5. A resistor is a two terminal device. It conducts equally in both 
directions [Fig. 8.1e].
6. A capacitor is a two terminal device. It stores some charge when 
dc voltage is applied [Fig. 8.1f].
PROCEDURE
1. A black rectangular shaped block having more than 3 legs may 
be IC.
2. A three terminal device: Connect central pin to red lead of the 
multimeter and any extreme pin to black lead of the multimeter.

ACTIVITY 9
AIM
 (i) Check whether the diode is in working order.
 (ii) Distinguish between npn and pnp transistor.
 (iii) Identify base, emitter, and collector of a transistor.
MATERIAL REQUIRED
A digital multimeter, a diode and a transistor.
PROCEDURE
1. To check a diode connect the black lead to ‘COM’ jack of 
multimeter and red lead to ‘V Ω mA’ jack. 
(i) Set the selector knob of digital multimeter in the diode mode 
( ). Connect the red lead (positive lead) of the multimeter 
to the anode of the diode and the black lead to the cathode 
of the diode (the cathode is always marked with a silver 
ring). The multimeter should show a reading in the range 
of ~0.4 – 0.8 forward voltage drop. If the reading is 0 then 
the diode is short circuited, it needs to be replaced. If the 
reading is 1 or over range, the diode  is open circuited. It 
should be replaced.
(ii) Reverse the diode connections with the multimeter (red lead 
to cathode, black lead to anode). The multimeter should 
show a reading of 1 or over range (indicating open circuit in 
reverse bias). If the multimeter reading is 0 then the diode 
is short circuited, it needs to be replaced.
2. (i) To distinguish between npn and pnp transistor set the 
selector knob of digital multimeter in diode mode. Connect 
the red lead of the multimeter to the central terminal of the

transistor and the black lead of the multimeter to any one 
of the extreme terminals of the transistor. If the multimeter 
displays a reading of ~0.4 – 0.8 (pn junction voltage drop), the 
junction is fine, and the central pin is p and outer terminal is 
n. If it shows any other reading then the junction is damaged. 
Check the voltage drop across the central terminal and the 
other outer terminal, if the reading is between ~0.4 – 0.8 
the junction is fine and the central pin is p and the outer 
terminal is n. This implies that the transistor is an npn 
transistor.
(ii) Repeat the experiment with the black lead of the multimeter 
connected to the central pin and red lead connected to the 
outer terminal consecutively. If the readings for both the 
cases is in the range of ~0.4 – 0.8 then the transistor is a 
pnp transistor.
(iii) The central pin is the base and the outer ones will be the 
collector and an emitter.
3. (i) To identify base, emitter and collector of a transistor. It is 
not possible to distinguish between the emitter and collector 
using the diode range of the multimeter.
 (ii) One can refer to the datasheet for the specific transistor. 
The manufacturer of the transistor gives the complete pin 
outs and the specifications of the transistor in its datasheet. 
One can also use the current gain (hfe) measurement 
setting of the multimeter to find the collector and emitter 
terminals. Set the multimeter in the hfe range and connect 
the transistor in the npn/pnp socket (depending on the types 
detected in the previous steps) with the assumed collector, 
base and emitter in their marked socket. If the meter shows 
a low reading (<10), reverse the position of the collector and 
emitter, and again check the hfe value. The hfe value should 
be above 100. If hfe value is greater than 100 it indicates 
that the collector, base, emitter terminals are connected in 
correct position and hence collector, emitter and base of the 
given transistor has been identified as per the multimeter 
transistor socket markings.
RESULT 
1. A pn junction diode has been successfully tested and it is in 
working/not working order.
2. The transistor terminals were successfully identified as collector, 
base, emitter and distinguished as a npn or pnp device.

AIM
To observe the refraction and lateral deviation of a beam of light 
incident obliquely on a glass slab.
APPARATUS AND MATERIAL REQUIRED
Drawing board, rectangular glass slab, white sheet of paper, 
adhesive tape (cellotape), drawing pins, a metre scale, alpins, 
protractor, pencil and eraser.
PROCEDURE
1. Fix a white sheet of paper on the drawing board with the help of 
cellotape or drawing pins.
2. Place the slab lengthwise symmetrically 
at the centre of the paper sheet and mark 
its boundary ABCD (Fig. A10.1) on the 
paper with a sharp pencil.
3. Draw a normal at a point F on the face 
AB. Draw a line EF, representing the 
incident ray, making an angle i (the angle 
of incidence) with the normal.
4. Fix two alpins P and Q with sharp tips, 
about 8 to 10 cm apart, vertically on the 
line EF.
5. Observe the images of the two pins 
through the opposite face of the glass 
slab. Fix two more alpins R and S 
about 8 to 10 cm apart, vertically on 
the white paper sheet carefully with 
their tips in line with the tips of the 
images of P and Q. Take care that the 
tips of all the alpins appear to be on 
a straight line.
Fig. A 10.1: Refraction through a 
rectangular glass slab

alpins on the white paper sheet with a pencil. Draw a straight 
line GH, representing the emergent ray, passing through the 
points marked R and S, meeting the face CD at G.
 7. Draw the line FG to represent the refracted ray. Draw a normal 
at the point G on the face CD making an angle of emergence 
e with the normal. Measure the angle of incidence i and angle of 
emergence e  with a protractor. Write the values of these angles 
on the white paper sheet. Do you find some relation between

 8. Extrapolate EF forward to meet the face CD of the glass slab at

 9. Check if the emergent ray GH is parallel to the incident ray EF  
along the original direction. It is laterally deviated by a 
perpendicular distance OL. Measure the lateral deviation OL = d

 10. Repeat Steps 2 to 9 by changing the angle of incidence.
 11. Repeat the Steps 2 to 10 by using glass slabs of different 
thicknesses. Measure the lateral deviation and the thickness 
of the glass slab each time. Also write the values of ∠i  and ∠e 
on the white paper sheet each time.
 12. Record observations in tabular form with proper units. What 
inference do you draw from your observations?
CONCLUSION
1.  The ray of light emerging from a glass slab is parallel to the 
incident ray direction, but is laterally deviated.
2.  The lateral deviation of the emergent ray with respect to the 
incident ray is directly proportional to the thickness of the  
glass slab

ACTIVITY 11
AIM
To observe the polarisation of light using two polaroids.
APPARATUS AND MATERIAL REQUIRED
Two polaroid sheets, source of light/sunlight, card board, a pair of 
scissors, white paper and glue.
PROCEDURE
1. Hold one piece of polaroid with your hand and look through 
it at a bright object say a lighted bulb or a tubelight. Note the 
change in intensity of light of the bright object.
 Repeat the above with the other piece of polaroid.
2. Hold both the polaroids keeping them 10 –12 cm apart. Now look 
through the two polaroids at the same bright object and note 
the intensity of light.
3. Slowly rotate one of the polaroids keeping the other polaroid 
fixed. Note the change in intensity of bright object as you rotate 
the Polaroid. Find the two alignment of polaroids when the light 
is maximum and when it is minimum.
CONCLUSION
The plane of polarisation of the polaroids are parallel when the 
observed intensity of light is maximum and it is perpendicular when 
intensity of light is minimum.

To observe the diffraction of light due to a thin slit.
APPARATUS AND MATERIAL REQUIRED
Two razor blades, one adhesive tape/cellotape source of light (electric 
bulb/laser torch), a piece of black paper and a glass plate (10 cm×10 cm).
PROCEDURE
1. Make a fine, single slit using two razor blades. For this purpose, 
take a glass plate and fix black paper on top of it. Cut out a 
narrow slit in the central part of the black paper. Place two razor 
blades side by side, quite close to each other over this slit as 
shown in Fig. A 12.1

 2. Place a glowing clear electric lamp

 3. Alternatively, place the slit about

(i) To study nature and the size of the image formed by a convex 
lens (for different distances of the candle from the lens).
APPARATUS AND MATERIAL REQUIRED
Improvised optical bench setup, a candle, match box, a small candle 
stand, a convex lens of small focal length and a metre scale.
PROCEDURE
1. Obtain an approximate value of the focal length of the convex 
lens by focusing the image of a distant object. It can be found by 
obtaining a sharp image of Sun or a tree on a plain wall, on the 
other side of the lens and measuring the distance between the 
lens and the wall with a scale. This distance gives approximate 
value of the focal length, f of the convex lens.
Note: Do not look at the Sun through the lens to see its image as it 
will hurt your eyes.

AIM
(ii) To study the nature and size of the image formed by a 
concave mirror on a screen by using a candle and a screen (for 
different distances of the candle from the concave mirror).
APPARATUS AND MATERIAL REQUIRED
Improvised optical banch setup, candle, match box, a small 
candle stand, concave mirror of nearly 25 cm focal length and  
a metre scale.
PROCEDURE
1. Obtain an approximate value of the focal length of the concave 
mirror by focusing the image of a distant object. It can be found by 
obtaining a sharp image of the sun or a tree on a plane wall, or on 
a sheet of paper and measuring the distance between the mirror 
and the image with a scale. This distance is an approximate value 
of the focal length, F of the concave mirror. Twice of this focal 
length is an approximate value of the radius of curvature of the 
mirror.
2. Set the optical bench properly.
3. Fix the concave mirror on the mirror holder and place it near 
one end of the meter scale.
4. Mount a lighted candle vertically in such a way that tip of the 
bright flame reaches up to the level of pole of the mirror. Place 
the candle arrangement near the mirror.
5. Mount the screen on upright.
6. Move the candle slowly away from the mirror till the image of its 
flame is seen on the screen. Adjust the position of the screen till 
the image becomes distinctly visible.
7. Compare the size of the candle flame with the size of the image. 
Also note whether the image is erect or inverted.

Observation on the nature, size and position of image shows that:
1. The image moves away from the focus as the object moves towards 
the focus.
2. The size of the image increases as it moves away from the mirror.
3. If the object is placed between infinity and F the image formed 
by a concave mirror is real and inverted.

mounted vertically.

OPTICAL BENCH ASSEMBLING
1. Optical bench provided in the kit comprises of:
 (i) Four pieces of 50cm scales
 (ii) Interlocking pins – 4

 (iv) Sliding bases for uprights – 4

join the other two halves of one metre scale.
5. Place these two joined scales side by side and fasten their ends using 
two locking pins on both the ends.
6. Check the level of the two scale assembly with spirit level if required 
relocate the assembly or level it with the pieces of paper/cardboard.

slots provided at its bottom fits into the optical bench. Move the sliding 
base along the entire length of the bench to ensure smooth movement.

horizontal groove is to be used for holding screen.
